# What Is a Mutual Action Plan?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-mutual-action-plan/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-15 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Revenue

> Summary: A mutual action plan is a document both buyer and seller can see, listing the steps to a decision and go-live, each with a date and an owner. It exists because buying groups are large and revisit decisions: Gartner found 95% go back at least once. A plan only helps when the buyer has agreed it, dates are real and each change is recorded.

A mutual action plan (MAP) is a shared document, agreed by buyer and seller, that lists the steps to a purchase decision and the start of work, each with a date and a named owner. It turns a close date the seller hopes for into a sequence the buyer has accepted. A plan the buyer never confirmed is a forecast assumption, not a mutual plan.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## What a mutual action plan means

Deals often slip on steps nobody listed: a security review, a legal redline, a budget sign-off in another department. A MAP lists those steps in advance, in the buyer's order, each assigned to a person on one side or the other.

Outreach account executive Ryan Jander, in a 2021 company blog, calls it "a shared document that helps a buyer and seller collaborate on a shared buying process". His contents list includes a value summary, go-live dates, milestones, deadlines, an owner and outcomes. Aviso's product documentation calls it "a collaborative workspace designed to align buyers and sellers on key milestones", with buyer and seller roles and a due date on each action item.

| A mutual action plan is | It is not |
| --- | --- |
| Agreed with the buyer and visible to them | An internal close plan the buyer never sees |
| A list of buyer and seller steps, each with an owner | A list of the seller's tasks only |
| Dated backwards from the buyer's go-live or decision date | Dated forwards from the seller's quarter end |
| Updated as steps move, with changes kept | Rewritten so it always looks on track |

## Why it matters for a commercial team

Buying decisions are not linear. Gartner's buyer enablement research describes a typical buying group of six to ten stakeholders and six "buying jobs": problem identification, solution exploration, requirements building, supplier selection, validation and consensus creation. Gartner also found that 95% of buying groups go back to revisit decisions at least once as new information emerges. A plan must be able to record those loops.

Consensus is where deals stall. In a May 2025 release, Gartner reported that 74% of buyer teams in a survey of 632 B2B buyers showed "unhealthy conflict". Groups that reached consensus were 2.5 times more likely to report a high-quality deal. A MAP does not create consensus, but it shows which members of the [buying committee](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-buying-committee/) have taken part and which steps wait on them.

It also tests the forecast. A deal in Commit needs evidence, as set out in [What Is a Forecast Category?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-forecast-category/). Buyer procurement and legal steps dated inside the quarter are that evidence; blank steps are a warning.

In **lowob**'s model, the MAP is a shared record of commitments, and each change is a small decision. When the buyer moves the security review back two weeks, the plan should show the old date, the new date and the reason. Some tools sync the plan into the CRM; Trumpet's help pages say its MAP on the HubSpot deal record "stays in sync". The reasons for changes still need recording. [Supersede, Never Overwrite](https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/) applies to dates as much as to prices.

## How to build one

An illustrative MAP for a services engagement, dated backwards from the buyer's start date:

| Step | Owner | Side | Due | Evidence it is done |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Confirm problem and success measures | Head of operations | Buyer | Week 1 | Written success measures |
| Scoping workshop | Account lead | Seller | Week 2 | Agreed scope note |
| Proposal and pricing | Account lead | Seller | Week 3 | Proposal sent |
| Security and data review | IT lead | Buyer | Week 5 | Questionnaire returned |
| Commercial and legal terms | Procurement and counsel | Buyer | Week 6 | Redlines closed |
| Budget approval | Finance director | Buyer | Week 7 | Purchase order raised |
| Signature and kick-off date | Economic buyer | Buyer | Week 8 | Signed contract |

Write it with the buyer, not for them, working back from their decision date. Put buyer steps first, since sellers cannot control them. Review it at every meeting and record each date change with its reason.

Agents can draft the first version from past deals of the same type. Under **lowob**'s Gateway 1, the draft goes to the account lead before the client sees it, because a MAP sent in error commits the firm to dates the client never agreed.

## lowob takeaways

- **Mutual means the buyer agreed.** A plan the buyer has not confirmed is an assumption.
- **List buyer steps first.** Security, legal and budget approvals are where deals slip.
- **Keep the changes.** Every moved date is a small decision with a reason.
